doc.title: Etta Jones interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 2, 1998

title: Mother's pride and meeting Billie Holiday
summary: She met Holiday several times, including when Holiday came to hear her at the Onyx, and explains how singers move from their idol's influence to their own style.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: Was your mother happy with your career?
I think she was very proud.
And I assume that you got to meet Billie Holiday?

I met her at least three times. Once in Chicago she was leaving after one of the shows, a break, probably going somewhere to eat, and they introduced me to her, and I was just in heaven, and she had this big white fox fur on, and a big flower. Oh she was so beautiful, and my heart almost stopped beating. And then when I was at the Onyx Club on 52nd Street, she was working across the street and they must have told her, “This little girl over here that’s working over here sounds like you.” And she came and she stood by the cash register. I could see her over there listening. And I don’t know what she said or anything, but I was just, I don’t know why I wasn’t so nervous. Because when I met Thelma I asked her, “Do you hear any of you in me?” And she said, “Maybe.” I wanted to ask Billie Holiday do you hear any of— because I mean she was my idol so whatever I sang probably sounded like her.
But did you consciously say I’m going to sing this like I think Billie would sing it?

No. It just came out like that and then people say they still hear it now but now they say I came through it. And I figure if you’re a singer and you like someone, you’re going to sound something like them until — especially when you first start. And then after that you will come out of it yourself into your own self. You know you might have a little, still a little of them here and there, but you’ll have your own thing.
Well you have to learn from somewhere. You have to have something to aspire to. And I think it’s the same for saxophone players.
Find an influence and then move on.
